stack.text: Performance Benchmark Document
This document contains 50 paragraphs of text used to benchmark the lpdf layout engine. It exercises parse, layout, pagination splitting, and PDF rendering across roughly 20 pages.

Paragraph 1. The layout engine processes each node in the document tree, computing sizes and positions before emitting PDF content streams. Each text node is measured glyph by glyph using the advance width tables loaded from font metrics.

Paragraph 2. Pagination splits the resolved layout tree into per-page slices. The split algorithm recurses into Stack and Grid nodes, advancing the remaining space counter as each child is placed. When a child exceeds the remaining space it is carried to the next page.

Paragraph 3. The PDF writer emits content streams using pdf-writer, a low-level Rust crate designed for Typst. Each page produces one content stream containing text drawing operators and any image XObjects referenced by that page.

Paragraph 4. Font subsetting reduces embedded font data to only the glyphs actually used in the document. The subsetter crate processes TrueType font tables and rebuilds them with the minimal glyph set, keeping PDF file sizes small even for large character sets.

Paragraph 5. Color tokens are resolved at parse time from a fixed palette of semantic names such as primary, surface, text, and text-muted. Custom hex colors are passed through directly as RGB triples in the PDF color space.

Paragraph 6. The Stack primitive stacks its children vertically with configurable gap spacing. Children are sized to the full available width by default. A child may opt out of full-width sizing by declaring an explicit width or by being a Frame with centered alignment.

Paragraph 7. The Flank primitive places its children in a horizontal row. All children except the last take their natural width. The last child fills the remaining horizontal space. Vertical alignment of children is controlled by the align attribute.

Paragraph 8. The Split primitive distributes its children evenly across the full width with equal spacing between them. It is useful for building header rows with left-aligned and right-aligned sections separated by flexible whitespace.

Paragraph 9. The Grid primitive arranges children in a multi-column grid. The number of columns is specified by the cols attribute. Row heights are determined by the tallest child in each row. Cells may span multiple columns using the span attribute.

Paragraph 10. The Cluster primitive wraps children onto new rows when the available width is exhausted, similar to CSS flexbox with flex-wrap enabled. It is suited to tag lists, badge rows, and any collection of variably-sized inline elements.

Paragraph 11. The Frame primitive centers its single child both horizontally and vertically within a bounding box. It is commonly used for images, icons, and decorative shapes that need precise placement within a containing region.

Paragraph 12. The Divider primitive renders a horizontal or vertical rule. Its thickness, color, and orientation are configurable. It participates in stack layout as a zero-height separator, contributing only the rule pixels without additional gap spacing.

Paragraph 13. The Table primitive renders a bordered grid of cells using explicit row and cell markup. Column widths can be fixed, proportional, or auto-sized. Header rows marked with the header attribute are styled with a distinct background color.

Paragraph 14. The Text primitive renders a paragraph of inline content. Inline spans may override the font family, font size, color, and decoration of a text run. Hyperlinks are encoded as PDF URI actions on the span bounding box.

Paragraph 15. QR codes are generated at render time from a data string using the qrcode crate. The resulting binary matrix is written as a PDF XObject bitmap. The size attribute controls the output dimensions; the data attribute carries the encoded payload.

Paragraph 16. Barcodes are rendered as a series of filled rectangles in the PDF content stream. The engine computes bar widths from the Code 128 encoding of the input string and places bars at the correct positions within the declared bounding box.

Paragraph 17. Images are embedded using DCTDecode for JPEG inputs and FlateDecode for PNG inputs. RGBA PNG images require an additional SMask XObject for the alpha channel, which is built by splitting the interleaved RGBA pixel data into separate RGB and alpha planes.

Paragraph 18. The paginate attribute controls page break behavior at any node boundary. A value of no treats the node as an indivisible unit. A value of break-before forces a page break before the node. A value of break-after forces a break after it.

Paragraph 19. The keep-next value of paginate ensures that a node and its next sibling always begin on the same page. If both nodes fit on the current page they are placed normally. If the next sibling would overflow to the next page both nodes are bumped together.

Paragraph 20. Repeating page chrome is declared with the repeat attribute on any top-level child of the page. Nodes with repeat equal to page are rendered on every page of the document at the same position. They do not consume layout space in the normal flow.

Paragraph 21. The meta element carries document-level properties including title, author, subject, keywords, and creator. These values are written to the PDF information dictionary and are indexed by PDF viewers and search engines that inspect document metadata.

Paragraph 22. Encryption is applied as a post-processing pass on the raw PDF bytes after rendering. The RC4-128 algorithm encrypts string and stream objects in place. Because RC4 is length-preserving the cross-reference table offsets remain valid without rewriting.

Paragraph 23. The key derivation algorithm follows ISO 32000-1 section 7.6 for revision 3 of the standard security handler. An MD5 digest is computed from the padded owner password, the permission flags, and the file identifier to produce the 16-byte encryption key.

Paragraph 24. Permission flags restrict which operations a reader application may perform on the encrypted document. Supported flags include printing, content modification, text copying, annotation creation, form field filling, content accessibility, document assembly, and high-quality printing.

Paragraph 25. The WASM binary is built with wasm-bindgen and wrapped by thin adapter layers for Node and TypeScript, .NET and C#, PHP, and Python. Each adapter exposes the same three entry points: load font, load image, and render PDF.

Paragraph 26. The license system uses Ed25519 signature verification to validate a base64url-encoded token containing an expiry date and permitted domain. Tokens are generated offline with the private key and embedded in the adapter constructor call.

Paragraph 27. Design tokens map semantic size names to point values. The xs through xxl scale provides consistent spacing and font-size steps across all documents. Authors reference tokens by name rather than by absolute point values, keeping layouts portable across page sizes.

Paragraph 28. The snapshot test suite renders each fixture document to PDF bytes, computes the SHA-256 hash of the output, and compares it against a stored reference hash. Any change to the rendering pipeline that alters the byte-level output fails the test immediately.

Paragraph 29. Updating snapshots after an intentional rendering change requires setting the UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS environment variable before running the test suite. The test runner writes new hash files to the test snapshots directory and prints the updated values to standard output.

Paragraph 30. The schema file validates the XML structure of lpdf documents before parsing. It defines allowed elements, attributes, and their permitted values. Documents that fail schema validation produce a parse error with the offending element and attribute identified by name.

Paragraph 31. The core-wasi crate wraps the core library for WASI execution environments. It exposes the same rendering functionality through a file-descriptor-based interface rather than the WASM memory buffer interface used by the browser and Node adapters.

Paragraph 32. Composite fonts declared in the assets section associate a font name used in text nodes with raw font bytes loaded at runtime by the adapter. The layout engine uses the loaded advance-width tables to measure the font accurately during line breaking.

Paragraph 33. Line breaking distributes words across lines such that no line exceeds the available width. Words that are wider than the full available width are placed on their own line and allowed to overflow. There is no hyphenation or soft-break support.

Paragraph 34. Text alignment is applied per paragraph. Left alignment is the default. Center and right alignment adjust the horizontal origin of each line after line breaking is complete. Justified alignment stretches inter-word spaces to fill the line width exactly.

Paragraph 35. Borders are drawn as filled rectangles on the inner edge of the padding region. Each side can be styled independently with a thickness and color. Border radius rounds the outer corners of the border rectangle using Bezier curve approximations.

Paragraph 36. Background fills are drawn before content using a filled rectangle operator in the PDF content stream. The fill color is resolved from the design token palette or from a literal hex color. Transparent backgrounds produce no fill operator in the output stream.

Paragraph 37. Padding expands the inner content area of a node inward from its border edges. All four sides can be set independently or with a single shorthand value. Padding interacts with border radius to keep content clear of rounded corners.

Paragraph 38. The render tree JSON format exposes the fully resolved layout as a language-neutral data structure. Each node carries its absolute position and size, resolved colors, and any text content split into measured lines ready for direct rendering in any PDF library.

Paragraph 39. Adapter-layer caching stores the subsetted font bytes from a previous render call and reuses them when the same font and the same glyph set are requested again. This reduces per-document render time significantly for templates that repeat the same font with the same character coverage.

Paragraph 40. The demo HTML file embeds a live preview of every showcase document in a side-by-side XML editor and PDF viewer. Edits to the XML are sent to the WASM engine on every keystroke. The resulting PDF bytes are displayed in an embedded object element.

Paragraph 41. The PHP adapter wraps the WASM binary using the ext-wasm extension when available and falls back to a subprocess call through the WASI runtime when the extension is absent. Both paths expose the same PHP class interface for compatibility.

Paragraph 42. The Python adapter uses the wasmtime package to load and execute the WASM binary. The adapter class mirrors the TypeScript API, exposing load font, load image, set encryption, and render pdf as instance methods on an engine object.

Paragraph 43. The .NET adapter uses the Wasmtime.NET bindings to host the WASM module. Memory is transferred between managed and unmanaged address spaces using span-based APIs that avoid unnecessary copies. The adapter is available as a NuGet package.

Paragraph 44. The Node adapter ships as a scoped npm package containing the WASM binary inline. The package exposes a single async factory function that compiles the WASM module and returns an engine instance. Font and image bytes are passed as Buffer or Uint8Array values.

Paragraph 45. Continuous integration runs the full test suite on every pull request using a matrix of Rust toolchain versions. The WASM build is verified by compiling the package and running the adapter test suites for each language target in isolated containers.

Paragraph 46. The relayout CSS library inspired the set of layout primitives used in lpdf. The Stack, Flank, Split, Cluster, Grid, Frame, and Divider primitives map directly to their relayout counterparts, giving web developers an immediately familiar mental model.

Paragraph 47. PDF content streams use PostScript-style operators. Text is drawn with Tf to set the font, Td to advance the text matrix, and Tj to emit a string. Graphics use re for rectangles, f for fill, and S for stroke. The cm operator sets the current transform matrix.

Paragraph 48. The cross-reference table lists the byte offset of every indirect object in the PDF file. A reader uses these offsets to seek directly to any object without scanning the file sequentially. The table is located by reading the startxref value at the end of the file.

Paragraph 49. PDF trailers carry a dictionary with the total object count, the root catalog reference, the information dictionary reference, and the file identifier array. The identifier is a pair of MD5 hashes used to distinguish document versions and to derive encryption keys.

Paragraph 50. This final paragraph marks the end of the benchmark fixture. The document intentionally spans multiple pages to exercise the pagination splitting logic on a realistic workload. Each paragraph adds measurable parse, layout, and render cost to the total pipeline time.
